svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Google Cloud verifies an AWS credential using GetCallerIdentity without AWS-side configuration, how an attribute mapping turns an ARN into a subject and custom attributes, direct resource access compared with service account impersonation, and why a claims-based identity makes recreated identities indistinguishable
svg.title: Workload Identity Federation for AWS: no key, no service account, and no directory
svg.text: Google asks AWS who the caller is. The verification runs the opposite way round.
Workloads present the AWS credentials they already hold; Google verifies them via GetCallerIdentity.
And nothing changes on the AWS side
No role, no trust policy, no configuration changes in your AWS account for this option.
Nothing there records the trust.
One ARN becomes four separately grantable facts
arn:aws:sts::000000000000:assumed-role/ec2-my-role/i-00000000000000000
google.subject
the ARN — used in principal:// bindings, and appears in Cloud Logging
attribute.account
the AWS account ID
attribute.aws_role
the role name — grant to every workload in the role
attribute.aws_ec2_instance
the instance ID — grant to one machine
Direct resource access — RECOMMENDED
The principal IS the federated user.
No service account exists to be audited,
disabled, or handed Editor by accident.
Impersonation — the fallback
The principal is a Google Cloud service account.
For APIs with documented limitations only.
Not the default any more.
The catch: an identity with no directory — and the exact inverse of #39
Federation keeps no directory of accounts. It implements CLAIMS-BASED IDENTITIES: two tokens whose
claims map to the same google.subject are assumed to be the same user. There is no lookup.
Delete it, recreate it with the same name:
A Google service account (#39) → inherits NOTHING. Bindings use an immutable unique ID.
A federated identity → inherits EVERYTHING. Old and new are indistinguishable.
Google owns the identifier in one case and not the other — and says so rather than pretending.
So the guarantee moves into the mapping expression
Map NON-REUSABLE attributes · map IMMUTABLE ones (a user can edit theirs to match your binding)
· do not allow mappings to be modified · one provider per pool, to avoid subject collisions.
All four are one instruction: the identifier is yours to choose, and nobody downstream can check it.
Attribute conditions fail closed — accepted if true, otherwise REJECTED. Mirror of #36, where a deny applies when
it cannot decide. One subtracts access, the other admits an identity.
A key announced itself as dangerous by being a file. A mapping expression looks like configuration.
